'''GreenTech Automotive''' (also known as '''WM GreenTech Automotive Corp.''') was a United States automotive manufacturer founded in 2009 that planned to develop and produce ultralow-power [[electric car]]s resembling very small cars or large [[golf cart]]s. It was a [[Virginia]] corporation, with its operations based in [[Mississippi]].

Its founder and CEO was Charlie Wang. Between 2009 and 2013, GreenTech raised $141.5 million from Chinese investors, and $6 million from Mississippi and the state's [[Tunica County]], with the company promising to invest $60 million and create 350 jobs in the county. Wang promised to build a $2 billion plant in Mississippi, and said that the company planned to produce 250,000 cars a year and provide 4,500 local jobs at full production.

However, it produced few cars, if any. GreenTech declared bankruptcy in 2018, paying its investors and creditors only $7 million.

==History==
===2009–13===
[[File:Greentech T 3 2011.JPG|thumb|2011 Greentech T3]]
GreenTech Automotive was a Virginia corporation that was founded in 2009 by lawyer Charlie Wang (Xiaolin Wang), who was also its CEO. Its purpose was to manufacture, in rural [[Mississippi]], ultralow-power [[electric car]]s that resembled very small cars or large [[golf cart]]s.<ref>Trip Gabriel (August 9, 2013). [https://www.nytimes.com/2013/08/10/us/politics/hopefuls-connections-jolt-bitter-virginia-race.html?searchResultPosition=3 "Hopeful’s Connections Jolt Bitter Virginia Race,"] ''The New York Times''.</ref><ref name=denver>[https://www.denverpost.com/2013/08/11/electric-car-makers-aspirations-collide-with-reality/ "Electric car maker’s aspirations collide with reality ,"] ''The Denver Post'', June 6, 2016.</ref><ref name=live>Lou Kilzer (August 10, 2013).  [https://archive.triblive.com/local/local-news/greentechs-plans-doubted-from-start/ "GreenTech's plans doubted from start,"] ''Trib Live''.</ref><ref name=tyc>Craig Myers (October 17, 2009). [https://www.al.com/live/2009/10/former_front_man_for_chinese-a.html "Former front man for Chinese-American auto tycoon broke away, now race is on for investors, customers,"] AL.com.</ref><ref name=bacon>[https://www.baconsrebellion.com/where-did-140-million-in-greentech-money-go/ "Where Did $140 Million in GreenTech Money Go?,"] ''Bacon's Rebellion'', October 27, 2021.</ref>

The legal backstory to the GreenTech Automotive's creation took place months earlier, in connection with an electric car company similar to Greentech, [[Hybrid Kinetic Motors|Hybrid Kinetic Automotive Corp.]]<ref name=ab/> At that time, Charlie Wang was sued by a business partner of his with regard to control of Hybrid Kinetic Automotive. U.S. federal chief judge [[Michael P. Mills]] wrote in an opinion on the dispute that Wang had taken actions of "dubious legality" in issuing Hybrid Kinetic Automotive Corp. stock.<ref name=ab>[https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/complicated-legal-backstory-terry-mcauliffes-car-company/story?id=19959500 "The Complicated Legal Backstory of Terry McAuliffe's Former Car Company; A look at the dispute that gave rise to GreenTech,"] ''ABC News'', August 28, 2013.</ref><ref name=mills>Judge Michael P. Mills (June 23, 2009). [https://cases.justia.com/federal/district-courts/mississippi/msndce/3:2009cv00035/28896/136/0.pdf "Hybrid Kinetic Automotive Holdings v. Charles Wang et. al.,"] US District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi, Western Division.</ref> GreenTech was born out of the dispute.<ref name=ab/> Judge Mills noted that the company website described Wang as "a graduate of Duke Law School" who had formerly served as a "partner and the head of Asia practice for a prominent New York law firm <nowiki>[</nowiki>[[Cadwalader, Wickersham & Taft]]<nowiki>]</nowiki>" and who had, prior to that, held a similar position with a "prestigious Washington law firm"; however, the judge went on to comment that "While prominence and prestige are laudable attributes in today's society, the older virtues of common honesty and integrity sometimes still carry the day."<ref name=mills/><ref name=cause>[https://causeofaction.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/09/130922-REPORT-Final-GreenTech-Automotive-FINALIZED.pdf "Staff Investigative Report; GreenTech Automotive: A Venture Capitalized by Cronyism,"] ''Cause of Action'', September 2013, p. 9.</ref> Prior to the Hybrid Kinetic controversy, Wang had recently left Cadwalader, Wickersham & Taft after [[David Ji#Arrest by Chinese police, and detention by Changhong|allegedly forcing]] businessman [[David Ji]] to sign over control of Ji's electronics company to Wang's client, while Ji was held in custody in China.<ref name=cause/> The Hybrid Kinetic lawsuit was settled out of court with $1.5 million being paid to Wang's business partner, who also retained the name "Hybrid Kinetic," as Wang began aftesh using the "GreenTech" name.<ref name=ab/>

In October 2009, Wang promised to build a $2 billion plant in the [[Mississippi Delta]].<ref>[https://www.dispatch.com/story/business/2013/08/12/greentech-automotive-s-big-plans/23802828007/ "GreenTech Automotive's big plans haven't come to fruition,"] ''The Columbia Dispatch'', August 12, 2013.</ref> He announced that GreenTech planned to produce 250,000 cars a year at full production.<ref name=tyc/><ref>[https://www.al.com/live/2009/10/rival_to_proposed_baldwin_coun.html "Rival to proposed Bay Minette hybrid car plant unveils prototypes in Mississippi,"] AL.com., October 6, 2009.</ref>  Wang said "It will mean 4,500 jobs at full production," and that the company aspired to command at least one-third of the U.S. automotive market down the line.<ref>Robert Lee Long (October 6, 2009). [https://www.desototimes.com/news/greentech-unveils-tunica-car-plans/article_00259cb6-d546-507b-98cb-8cdbed92660f.html "GreenTech unveils Tunica car plans,"] ''DeSoto Times-Tribune''.</ref>

David Cole, the chairman of the [[Center for Automotive Research]], said Wang's claims were "very inflated from reality," and likely designed to attract investors.<ref name=tyc/>  Michelle Krebs, senior analyst at [[Edmunds (company)|edmunds]], which provides car research and reviews, said that demand for cars of that type was "extremely limited," given that many states did not permit such cars on their highways, and concluded: "What's the point?"<ref name=live/>

A March 2010 [[State Corporation Commission (Virginia)|Virginia State Corporation Commission]] document reported that GreenTech was owned 75% by Charlie Wang through a holding company that he owned, and 25% by businessman and politician [[Terry McAuliffe]] (who later became the [[Governor of Virginia]]); by 2012, McAuliffe had divested his interest.<ref name=bacon/><ref name=aud/>

Between 2009 and 2013, GreenTech raised $141.5 million from Chinese investors under the U.S. immigrant investor  [[EB-5]] program. That program gave foreigners a U.S. permanent residency [[green card]] if the foreigner invested $500,000 in a company that helped create jobs in a rural or high-unemployment area in the United States, if the $500,000 investment created “10 or more direct or indirect jobs.”<ref name=bacon/><ref>Christopher Jensen (February 11, 2010). [https://archive.nytimes.com/wheels.blogs.nytimes.com/2010/02/11/green-cards-for-green-cars/?searchResultPosition=5 "Green Cards for Green Cars,"] ''The New York Times''.</ref> As of August 2013, however, out of 91 foreign investors in GreenTech, only one had received permanent residency status.<ref name=gu/> Incentive financing in GreenTech from the [[state of Mississippi]] and [[Tunica County]], Mississippi, added up to another $6 million.<ref name=bacon/>

In May 2010, GreenTech acquired Hong Kong-based [[EuAuto Technology]] and its [[GTA Mycar|Mycar]] vehicle, a [[neighborhood electric vehicle]] with a top speed of 25 mph (40 km/h), and relocated the company's operations to the United States.<ref name=ste/> GreenTech's first manufacturing facility was temporarily in [[Horn Lake, Mississippi]].<ref>Robert Lee Long (July 29, 2011). [https://www.desototimes.com/news/greentech-to-begin-production/article_63ce154a-fda0-5955-9bb1-ccd19b60d59f.html "Greentech to begin production; October timetable disclosed,"] ''DeSoto Times-Tribune''.</ref> The company declined an [[Associated Press]] request to tour the Horn Lake manufacturing facility.<ref name=gu>[https://www.gulflive.com/mississippi-press-news/2013/08/mississippi_electric_car_compa.html "Mississippi electric car company's big plans haven't materialized with foreign investors,"] ''Gulf Live'', August 11, 2013.</ref>

[[Watchdog.org]] articles about GreenTech led, according to GreenTech, to federal investigations and negative attention.<ref name=ien/> In 2013 GreenTech sued the [[Franklin Center for Government and Public Integrity]], a nonprofit investigative-journalism organization, and its website Watchdog.org (as well as a journalist for the company), in federal court for $85 million for [[libel]] (noting among other things the website's characterization of GreenTech's company headquarters as "a broom closet"). However, GreenTech's lawsuit was dismissed.<ref name=ien/><ref>Jim Geraghty (April 17, 2013). [https://www.nationalreview.com/2013/04/greentech-vs-watchdogorg-jim-geraghty/ "GreenTech vs. Watchdog.org,"] ''The National Review''.</ref><ref>[https://patch.com/virginia/herndon/bp--the-greentech-automotive-inc-v-watchdogorg-libel-suit "The GreenTech Automotive, Inc. v. Watchdog.org Libel Suit; The electric car company founded by Terry McAuliffe has sued a local non-profit for libel. Is this lawsuit an attempt to suppress free speech?"], ''Patch'', May 2, 2013.</ref>

===2014–2020===
GreenTech merged with fledgling [[VL Automotive]] in 2014, intending to develop a traditionally powered version of the [[Fisker Karma]], called the [[WM Destino]].<ref>{{cite web|title=GreenTech Scatters New Seeds|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/05/18/automobiles/greentech-scatters-new-seeds.html?_r=0|website=The New York Times|access-date=28 May 2015|date=16 May 2014|first=Jim|last=Motavalli|url-access=limited}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Destino's VL Automotive merges with GreenTech Automotive|url=https://www.autoblog.com/2014/05/06/destinos-vl-automotive-merges-with-greentech-automotive/?guccounter=1|website=Autoblog|access-date=6 June 2015|date=6 May 2014|first=Sebastian|last=Blanco}}</ref> Also in 2014, Greentech was enmeshed in litigation in the [[Eastern District of Michigan]]  against [[Plastech Engineered Products|Plastech Holding Corp.]], which said that GreenTech  intentionally interfered with Plastech's relationship with Chinese carmaker [[JAC Motors]], and that Wang had met with Plastech about serving as the middleman in its deal, and "knew perfectly well that we had an agreement and interfered with it."<ref>[https://www.plasticsnews.com/article/20141112/NEWS/141119977/plastech-in-legal-battle-over-chinese-electric-car-contract "Plastech in legal battle over Chinese electric car contract,"] ''Plastics News'', November 12, 2014.</ref>

In 2016, Barbara Tuchel, who had been a candidate for the Tunica County Board of Supervisors, looking over the vacant site of what had been promised to be a new GreenTech production facility in [[Tunica County, Mississippi|Tunica County]], Mississippi, and said: "Welcome to GreenTech. Isn't this ridiculous?"<ref name=denver/> That same year, Wang said that construction of the Tunica building had been delayed by unstable soil in the region, but that "By the end of this year, the whole state-of-the-art facility will be done."<ref name=denver/> The facility was shut down in January 2017.<ref name=ste>{{cite web|url=https://www.greencarreports.com/news/1108421_greentech-auto-shutters-its-doors-closes-mississippi-factory|title=GreenTech shutters its doors, closes its Mississippi factory|date=19 January 2017 |work=Green Car Reports|author=Stephen Edelstein |access-date=13 June 2024}}</ref><ref name=pol/>

GreenTech had committed to invest $60 million in a Mississippi manufacturing plant, but it produced few cars–if any.<ref name=bacon/>   [[State Auditor of Mississippi|Mississippi State Auditor]] [[Stacey Pickering]] began a review in 2016 that found documentation reflecting only $3 million spent by GreenTech on automotive assembly equipment and parts.<ref name=bacon/>  While the company had also promised to create 350 full-time jobs, it was found to never have created more than 94 active, full-time jobs in Mississippi at any time.<ref name=bacon/><ref name=pol/>  Three employees at the Horn Lake facility said that GreenTech management sometimes asked workers to make believe that they were assembling cars when potential investors visited the facility, usually from China, and that employees would remove parts from earlier assembled cars and reattach them.<ref name=denver/> As one described it: "We would just be standing there acting like we were doing something. But it was pre-planned ... It was like a show."<ref name=denver/>

In July 2017, Mississippi State Auditor Pickering demanded that GreenTech and Charlie Wang pay Mississippi $6 million, because Greentech had not lived up to its promises to invest $60 million and create 350 jobs in Tunica County.<ref name=pol/><ref name=aud>[https://journalrecord.com/2017/07/06/mississippi-demands-6-4m-back-from-electric-car-maker-ceo/ "Mississippi demands $6.4M back from electric car maker, CEO,"] ''The Journal Record'', July 6, 2017.</ref> The auditor said: "I would venture that there isn't really much of an operation in Tunica at all. This appears to have been a game of smoke and mirrors, and a corporate entity that never had any intention to deliver on the promises it made."<ref name=aud/>   In November 2017, Mississippi Attorney General [[Jim Hood]] sued the company.<ref name=pol/> The company made only one, single $150,000 payment to the state of Mississippi.<ref name=bacon/>

Also in November 2017, a total of 32 Chinese investors in the company brought a $17 million [[fraud]] lawsuit against Greentech, McAuliffe, Charlie Wang,  [[Anthony Rodham]] (a brother of [[Hillary Clinton]]), and other company executives in a [[Fairfax County, Virginia]] court.<ref name=suit/><ref name=pol/> The lawsuit accused McAuliffe, Wang, and Rodham of lies, manipulation, [[fraudulent misrepresentation]]s,  and running a "scam."<ref name=pol/><ref name=suit>[https://www.politico.com/f/?id=00000160-028c-d90d-a367-de9e90610000 "Xia Bi et. al. v. Terry McAuliffe et. al.,"] Circuit Court of Fairfax County, November 22, 2017.</ref> The investors said that they were each swindled out of $560,000.<ref name=pol/><ref name=suit/>  They also said that as a result they risked being [[deported]] from the U.S. because the [[Department of Homeland Security]] had determined that Greentech had not generated the number of jobs necessary for the number of visas that were issued through the EB-5 program.<ref name=suit/><ref name=pol>Josh Gerstein (November 28, 2017). [https://www.politico.com/story/2017/11/28/greentech-automotive-lawsuit-terry-mcauliffe-262771 "Chinese investors sue McAuliffe, Rodham over green-car investments ,"] ''Politico''.</ref>  In June 2017 the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit]] upheld a ruling from a lower court federal judge, who said that the lawsuit was not specific enough about how the allegedly misleading and false statements induced the Chinese nationals to invest in Greentech; at the same time, the court of appeals noted that it strongly disapproved of the claims the defendants had made in promoting  Greentech.<ref>Josh Gerstein (November 28, 2017). [https://www.politico.com/story/2017/11/28/greentech-automotive-lawsuit-terry-mcauliffe-262771 "Appeals court won’t reopen suit against McAuliffe, Tony Rodham,"] ''Politico''.</ref>

GreenTech declared [[Chapter 11]] bankruptcy in February 2018.<ref>Ned Oliver (February 27, 2018). [https://richmond.com/news/local/government-politics/greentech-the-electric-car-company-once-led-by-mcauliffe-files/article_bf83ede4-ae12-5561-ad3b-b0a29c2b0984.html "GreenTech, the electric car company once led by McAuliffe, files for bankruptcy,"] ''Richmond Times-Dispatch.''</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/greentech-automotive-files-for-bankruptcy-1519775795|title=GreenTech Automotive Files for Bankruptcy|last=Yerak|first=Becky|date=28 February 2018|work=The Wall Street Journal|access-date=2020-02-06|language=en-US|issn=0099-9660}}</ref> It maintained that it had only minimal assets when it filed for bankruptcy.<ref name=bacon/> The bankruptcy filing noted that $7.5 million had been won by 12 investors who had sued the company, and that the company faced further  pending lawsuits.<ref name=ien>[https://www.ien.com/product-development/news/20994287/exgovernors-ev-company-files-for-bankruptcy "Ex-Governor's EV Company Files for Bankruptcy; Investors have called it a 'scam perpetrated by savvy and politically connected operatives,'"] ''Industrial Equipment News'', February 28, 2018.</ref> In a 2020 final settlement, GreenTech paid investors and creditors only $7 million.<ref name=bacon/>  Mississippi and Tunica County recovered only $575,000.<ref name=bacon/>

==Products==
* [[GTA Mycar]], a 2-door, 2-seater [[Neighborhood Electric Vehicle]] designed in 2003 by [[Giorgetto Giugiaro]], and developed by [[EuAuto Technology]]
